newsitem.title: USA: U.S West Coast crudes rise, local diffs flat.
newsitem.headline: U.S West Coast crudes rise, local diffs flat.

text.p: U.S. West Coast crude prices rose midday Thursday in line with a futures market that strengthened on reports of fresh tensions between Iraq and the United Nations (U.N).
U.N oil monitors were arrested in Northern Iraq by a Kurdish faction, according to the report, issued by the BBC Monitoring Servce.
The reports revived dull trade on the NYMEX crude oil futures exchange, with market players speculating the arrests could jeopardize oil-for-food supplies from Iraq.
On the West Coast, May crude trade appeared over, as players spent the morning requesting shipping space on ARCO's Line 63 pipeline, traders said.
ARCO expects to announce its shipping allotments on the line early Friday.

Sales of Alaskan North Slope (ANS) crude remained flat Thursday, with buyers speculating that BP Oil's below-average spot sales for May was forcing them to ship crude to the U.S. Gulf or build inventories in Alaska.
BP declined to comment on its shipping policies.
Meanwhile, inventory levels remained "normal" at Alaska's Valdez terminal, where ANS is stored before being shipped south, said an official for Alyeska Pipeline Service Co, the terminal's operator.
"By no means are we maxed out at the terminal," the official said, noting the 9.18 million-barrel-capacity of the tanks was only 62 percent filled.
Outright prices for May ANS stood 50 cents higher than yesterday in line with increases in spot May WTI.
On a notional basis, Line 63 was talked $2.37/2.27 under May West Texas Intermediate/Cushing (WTI). The grade rarely trades off WTI.
Traders reported no deals in Line 63 and heavy California grades.
